P4Q1: Examines whether God's Incarnation was fitting, whether necessary for man's restoration, whether it would have occurred without sin, and its proper timing in salvation history.
P4Q2: Explains the union of divine and human natures in Christ's one Person, unconfused, not accidental, but a real union in the Person brought about by grace, not nature.
P4Q3: Considers which divine Person could assume human nature, showing assumption properly belongs to a Person, and why the Son alone actually became incarnate.
P4Q4: Discusses why human nature, not another creature, was assumable by God, and why the Word assumed an individual human nature descended from Adam, not an abstract or universal one.
P4Q5: Affirms Christ assumed a true body, a true rational soul, and a human intellect, against heresies denying the reality of His flesh or mind.
P4Q6: Argues the Word assumed the whole human nature simultaneously, not soul before flesh in time, though there is a natural order among the parts assumed.
P4Q7: Shows Christ's soul possessed habitual grace, all the virtues, gifts, and prophetic knowledge in their fullest and unsurpassable degree, though not faith or hope.
P4Q8: Explains Christ as Head of the Church, of all mankind, and even of the angels, from whom grace flows into the members of His mystical body.
P4Q9: Establishes that Christ possessed, besides Divine knowledge, three kinds of created human knowledge: beatific, infused, and acquired, since He had a true, complete human soul.
P4Q10: Christ's soul saw the Divine Essence in the beatific vision but did not comprehend it, knowing all things in the Word more clearly than any other creature.
P4Q11: Christ's soul had a divinely infused knowledge, in distinct habits, enabling Him to know all things expressible in human concepts without needing to reason discursively.
P4Q12: Christ possessed acquired, experiential knowledge through His own senses and active intellect, and truly advanced in it, though not in His infused or beatific knowledge.
P4Q13: Christ's human soul, though instrumentally united to the Word, was not itself omnipotent; it had full power over His own body and, as the Word's instrument, worked miracles.
P4Q14: Christ voluntarily assumed real bodily defects like hunger, thirst, weariness, and death, not contracted from Adam, to satisfy for sin and prove His true humanity.
P4Q15: Christ took on true passions such as sorrow, fear, pain, and wonder but was without sin or its sinful inclination, being simultaneously wayfarer and comprehensor.
P4Q16: Analyzes propositions like "God is man" and "man is God," clarifying how divine and human predicates rightly apply to Christ through the communication of idioms.
P4Q17: Teaches that although Christ has two natures, He is one Person with, properly speaking, one personal being, since human nature adds no distinct act of existence.
P4Q18: Christ possessed two distinct wills, divine and human (including sensory appetite), always concordant, against Monothelite heretics who claimed He had only one will.
P4Q19: Christ had distinct divine and human operations corresponding to His two natures and wills, and His human acts were truly meritorious both for Himself and for others.
P4Q20: As man, Christ is subject to the Father in goodness, power, and obedient will, yet this subjection does not make Him subject to Himself as God.
P4Q21: Christ prayed according to His human will and sensuality, presenting His human desires to the Father; His rightly ordered prayers were always heard.
P4Q22: Christ is the one true priest, both offerer and victim, whose sacrifice expiates sin, benefits Himself and others, and endures forever after the order of Melchisedech.
P4Q23: Considers divine adoption of rational creatures as sons through grace, concluding this term is not properly applied to Christ as man, since He is the natural Son of God.
P4Q24: Christ, as man, was eternally predestined to be Son of God by the grace of union; His predestination serves as both exemplar and cause of the elect's predestination.
P4Q25: Christ's humanity, united hypostatically to the Word, is rightly adored with the supreme worship due to God alone; His cross and images receive only relative honor.
P4Q26: Christ alone, as man, is properly the Mediator between God and men, reconciling humanity to God by uniting both natures and offering Himself in satisfaction for sin.
P4Q27: Mary was sanctified in the womb before birth, cleansed from the stain of original sin, and after Christ alone received such a singular privilege of grace.
P4Q28: Affirms Mary's perpetual virginity before, during, and after Christ's birth, against heretics who denied her virginal conception or her subsequent lifelong chastity.
P4Q29: Explains why it was fitting that Christ be born of an espoused virgin, truly married to Joseph, for the sake of Christ, Mary, and the faithful.
P4Q30: Argues it was fitting that an angel announce Christ's conception to Mary beforehand, in a bodily apparition, following a reverently ordered sequence of events.
P4Q31: Christ's flesh was truly derived from Adam through David's line and the Virgin's purest blood, tracing a real, though sinlessly assumed, human lineage.
P4Q32: The Holy Ghost is attributed as the active cause forming Christ's body from the Virgin's blood, while Mary herself cooperated only passively, not actively, in the conception.
P4Q33: Christ's body was instantly formed and animated in the same moment of conception, a supernatural yet truly natural generation accomplished without human seed.
P4Q34: Christ was sanctified, possessed the use of free will, was able to merit, and was already a perfect comprehensor in the very first instant of His conception.
P4Q35: Discusses Christ's true temporal birth from Mary, His painless delivery, Mary's title as Mother of God, and the fitting time and place, Bethlehem, of His birth.
P4Q36: Christ's birth was revealed selectively—to shepherds, Magi, and a few chosen others—through angels and a star, rather than proclaimed openly to all people at once.
P4Q37: Christ was fittingly circumcised, given His name, and presented in the temple to fulfill the Law, prove His true flesh, and set an example of obedience.
P4Q38: John's baptism, though instituted by God, conferred no sanctifying grace itself but prepared for Christ's baptism, and its authority ceased once Christ's own baptism began.
P4Q39: Christ was fittingly baptized by John in the Jordan to sanctify the waters, and at His baptism the Trinity was manifested by the Father's voice and the descending dove.
P4Q40: Christ lived publicly among men, embraced poverty and a measured austerity, and observed the Law, fitting His manner of life to His mission of teaching and redeeming.
P4Q41: Christ willingly allowed Himself to be tempted in the desert after His fast, to strengthen believers against temptation and to exemplify resistance to the devil.
P4Q42: Christ's preaching was directed first to the Jews, delivered openly rather than committed to writing, to fulfill ancient promises before extending to the Gentiles.
P4Q43: Christ worked miracles by His own divine power to confirm the divine origin of His teaching, beginning publicly at Cana, and sufficiently proving His Godhead.
P4Q44: Christ fittingly worked miracles on demons, heavenly bodies, men, and irrational creatures, each ordered to manifest His saving power over every order of creation.
P4Q45: Christ was transfigured to strengthen the disciples' faith before His Passion, giving a foretaste of resurrection glory, witnessed by chosen apostles and confirmed by the Father's voice.
P4Q46: Christ's suffering was not absolutely necessary but fitting for man's deliverance; He truly suffered the greatest bodily and spiritual pain, at a fitting time, place, and manner.
P4Q47: Christ died both from His own will and at the hands of persecutors; the Father delivered Him up, and His killers, though sinning gravely, acted partly in ignorance.
P4Q48: Christ's Passion caused salvation by way of merit, satisfaction, sacrifice, and redemption, and efficiently produced grace as an instrument of His divine power.
P4Q49: Through His Passion Christ freed us from sin, the devil's power, and punishment, reconciled us to God, opened heaven, and merited His own exaltation.
P4Q50: Christ truly died, His soul separating from His body while His Godhead remained united to both; His death itself conduced positively to human salvation.
P4Q51: Christ's burial confirmed the truth of His death and, His body remaining incorrupt, prefigured hope of resurrection, lasting one day and two nights in the tomb.
P4Q52: Christ's soul descended into hell after death, delivering the holy patriarchs from limbo, though not the damned or unbaptized infants, illuminating but not emptying hell entirely.
P4Q53: It was necessary and fitting for Christ to rise again on the third day, being the first to rise from death, and He rose by His own divine power.
P4Q54: Christ's risen body was a true, glorified, and entire body, and He retained His wounds as trophies of victory and proofs of the Resurrection's reality.
P4Q55: Christ's Resurrection was shown only to chosen witnesses through convincing proofs, not to all people, so as to strengthen the disciples' testimony without compelling belief.
P4Q56: As the first and exemplary cause, Christ's Resurrection is the efficient cause both of the future bodily resurrection of the dead and of the spiritual resurrection of souls.
P4Q57: Christ fittingly ascended bodily above all the heavens by His own power after the Resurrection, and His Ascension is itself a cause of our salvation.
P4Q58: Christ, both as God essentially and, derivatively, as man, is said to sit at the Father's right hand, signifying eternal beatitude and supreme judiciary power.
P4Q59: Christ, as man, was given full judiciary power over all human affairs and even the angels, a power He merited and will fully exercise at the final judgment.
P4Q60: Defines a sacrament as a sign of a sacred, sanctifying reality, necessarily sensible, employing determinate matter and words to signify the grace it confers.
P4Q61: Sacraments suit human nature's need for sensible signs of spiritual realities and were necessary in every age, though differing in kind before sin, after sin, and after Christ.
P4Q62: The New Law's sacraments truly cause grace instrumentally, deriving their power from Christ's Passion, unlike the Old Law's sacraments which only signified grace without conferring it.
P4Q63: Certain sacraments imprint an indelible spiritual character, a share in Christ's own priesthood, on a power of the soul, deputing the recipient to divine worship.
P4Q64: God alone works the interior sacramental effect while ministers act only instrumentally; sacraments are instituted by God alone and can be validly administered even by unworthy ministers.
P4Q65: There are fittingly seven sacraments, ordered to perfect the spiritual life and remedy sin's defects, with the Eucharist greatest, though not all equally necessary for salvation.
P4Q66: Baptism is washing with water in the Trinitarian form, instituted after Christ's Passion, never to be repeated, with water, blood, and Spirit as its three modes.
P4Q67: Ordinarily bishops and priests solemnly baptize, but in cases of necessity any person, even an unbaptized layperson or a woman, can validly confer Baptism.
P4Q68: All persons, including infants and the mentally incapacitated, are obliged and fit to receive Baptism, which is necessary for salvation apart from extraordinary exception.
P4Q69: Baptism remits all sin and its punishment, confers grace and virtues, incorporates one into Christ, and opens heaven, though insincerity can impede its effect until removed.
P4Q70: Old Testament circumcision prefigured Baptism as a sign of faith and was fittingly instituted, but unlike Baptism it did not itself confer sanctifying grace.
P4Q71: Catechism and exorcism fittingly precede Baptism, instructing the candidate in faith and expelling the devil's power, and are properly performed by a priest.
P4Q72: Confirmation, using consecrated chrism applied to the forehead by a bishop, imprints a character and bestows grace for spiritual maturity and strength in professing the faith.
P4Q73: The Eucharist, spiritual food necessary for the perfect Christian life, was fittingly instituted at the Last Supper, prefigured by the Old Testament Paschal Lamb.
P4Q74: The proper matter of the Eucharist is wheaten bread and grape wine mixed with a little water, against various erroneous historical substitutions of matter.
P4Q75: By transubstantiation the whole substance of bread and wine is instantaneously converted into Christ's Body and Blood, known only through faith, while their accidents remain unchanged.
P4Q76: The whole Christ is truly present under each species and every part of it, not locally but sacramentally by concomitance, imperceptible to any bodily eye.
P4Q77: The accidents of bread and wine remain miraculously without a subject after consecration, retaining their natural powers to nourish, corrupt, and be divided.
P4Q78: The words "This is My body" and "This is the chalice of My blood" are the proper consecratory forms, true and effective through Christ's own power.
P4Q79: The Eucharist confers grace, forgives venial and even mortal sin under contrition, remits some temporal punishment, preserves from future sin, and leads toward final glory.
P4Q80: Distinguishes sacramental from spiritual eating; only the just profit fully, sinners who receive unworthily sin gravely, and frequent, even daily, communion is lawful though not obligatory.
P4Q81: Christ Himself first received His own Body and Blood before giving it to the apostles, including Judas, in His still passible, not yet glorified, body.
P4Q82: Consecration and lawful dispensation of the Eucharist belong properly to priests alone; even sinful or heretical priests, though sinning, can still validly consecrate.
P4Q83: The Mass re-presents Christ's sacrifice through fittingly ordered words, actions, times, and vessels, with the Church's statutes covering any incidental defects in its celebration.
P4Q84: Penance is a true sacrament remitting sin committed after Baptism through contrition, confession, and satisfaction, necessary for salvation and repeatable throughout life as a "second plank."
P4Q85: Penance, as an act of will grieving over sin one has committed, is a special virtue, a species of justice, though it may also arise initially from fear.
P4Q86: Penance forgives all confessed and contrite mortal sins together, removing guilt entirely, though a debt of temporal punishment may still remain to be satisfied.
P4Q87: Venial sin, unlike mortal sin, can be remitted outside formal Penance by fervent acts of charity or sacramentals like holy water, without a separate mortal sin.
P4Q88: Previously forgiven sins can be said to "return" through subsequent grave ingratitude, restoring their debt of punishment, though not literally reviving the original personal guilt.
P4Q89: Through Penance, infused grace and all the virtues once lost by mortal sin are restored, and even good deeds "deadened" by later sin are revived.
P4Q90: Contrition, confession, and satisfaction are fittingly assigned as the integral parts of Penance, with distinct kinds before Baptism, for mortal sin, and for venial sin.
